prompt.context: Our client owns an antique store in downtown Chicago that could not meet its sales targets. To attract customers, the owners (a couple) began making home-made sandwiches. Over time the sandwiches became famous in the area, boosting profits. The store now earns revenue from both antiques and food (sandwiches, desserts, chips, and drinks). The owners want to expand by opening new stores but are unsure whether this is a good strategy.
prompt.question: Develop a growth strategy for the client. Consider the costs involved and the key business drivers. Should they open new stores, and if so, how?

clarifying_info.q: What proportion of revenue comes from lunch versus other times?
clarifying_info.a: 75% of revenue is generated during lunch; the remaining 25% comes after 1pm.

clarifying_info.q: How is the store utilized throughout the day?
clarifying_info.a: The store is fully utilized during lunch and under-utilized at other times.

clarifying_info.q: What is the revenue breakdown by product?
What are the main cost drivers?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs: raw materials, labor, and processing. Fixed costs: rent, SG&A, insurance, and depreciation.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a delivery service currently?

clarifying_info.a: Mostly working people seeking a quick lunch; also some non-working people and students.
Restaurants in the surrounding area serving primarily from 11:30am to 1:30pm.

framework: Understand the current business: revenue mix (food vs. antiques), cost structure, peak vs. off-peak utilization
Assess market and competitive context: customer segments, competitor landscape, brand differentiators (home-made sandwiches, antique atmosphere)
Evaluate growth directions: (1) internal business optimization, (2) vertical integration, (3) diversification (related/unrelated), (4) new geographic areas
Evaluate growth modes: (1) internal resources, (2) alliances/partnerships, (3) M&A
Analyze feasibility constraints: downtown Chicago real-estate availability and high rents, need to reach break-even quickly
Develop prioritized recommendations and identify risks

questions.prompt: What are the key customer and competitive dynamics the client must understand before deciding to expand?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify that customers are time-constrained working professionals seeking quick, quality food; competitors are nearby restaurants with a narrow lunch window; the client's differentiation is the home-made sandwich reputation and unique antique-store atmosphere. Candidates should note the importance of protecting brand equity during any expansion.

questions.prompt: Walk through the possible directions and modes of growth for this client.
questions.guidance: Direction options: (1) Optimize the existing store (e.g., add delivery to capture off-peak demand and expand customer base); (2) Vertical integration (e.g., supply sandwiches to grocery stores or other fast-food outlets); (3) Diversification into related products beyond sandwiches; (4) Open new stores in new geographic areas (other Chicago locations or other major cities). Mode options: internal resources (slow but full control), alliances/franchising (faster, shared risk), M&A (fastest but costly and complex). Candidates should evaluate each option against feasibility given high downtown Chicago rents and scarcity of suitable storefronts.

questions.prompt: What are the practical constraints on opening new downtown Chicago stores, and how might the client work around them?
questions.guidance: Key constraints: high rents in downtown Chicago, difficulty finding available stores, need for quick break-even. Workarounds: consider smaller-format or non-antique-decorated kiosks/counters in Chicago; expand to strategic locations in other major U.S. cities with a flagship one-store-per-city model; explore B2B channels (supplying sandwiches to offices, groceries, or caterers) to grow revenue without opening new retail locations.

questions.prompt: How could the client increase revenue from the existing store without opening new locations?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm: (1) Add delivery service to serve lunch customers who cannot come in and to utilize off-peak capacity; (2) Expand the menu beyond sandwiches (catering, breakfast items, dinner specials) to shift the 75/25 lunch/non-lunch split; (3) Corporate catering orders for nearby offices; (4) Sell branded/packaged sandwiches or recipes to grocery chains.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does the client have to grow revenue and profitability, beyond simply opening replica stores?

categories.name: Optimize existing store
ideas: Add a delivery service to capture off-peak demand
Introduce breakfast or dinner menu items to reduce lunch-hour concentration
Offer catering packages to nearby offices
Extend hours or add events (e.g., antique viewing evenings)

categories.name: New store formats
ideas: Open smaller kiosk/counter formats inside office buildings or food halls
Operate a non-antique-decorated satellite location to test lower-rent areas
Partner with existing cafes or delis to co-brand a sandwich station

categories.name: B2B / wholesale channels
ideas: Supply sandwiches to grocery stores under the store's brand
Partner with fast-food chains or food courts to distribute the product
Offer private-label catering for corporate clients

categories.name: Geographic expansion
ideas: One flagship store per major city (New York, Los Angeles, Boston) to preserve exclusivity
Franchise the model to reduce capital requirements
License the brand and recipes to operators in other markets

categories.name: Product diversification
ideas: Expand food offerings by location and customer base (e.g., health-focused items near gyms)
Sell antique merchandise online to monetize the original business more broadly
Offer cooking classes or branded merchandise around the home-made sandwich concept

recommendation: The client should pursue a multi-track growth strategy: (1) immediately add a delivery service to monetize off-peak capacity in the existing store, (2) explore B2B/wholesale channels (supplying sandwiches to groceries or offices) as a low-capital growth lever, and (3) selectively open one flagship store in one additional major U.S. city per year to maintain brand scarcity and quality control.
Downtown Chicago expansion should be limited given high rents and scarce real estate; non-antique-format kiosks are a secondary option to test if downtown demand justifies it.
risks: Brand dilution if expansion compromises the home-made quality or antique atmosphere
Inability to break even quickly in new high-rent locations
Operational complexity of managing multiple store formats or delivery logistics
Key-person dependency if the couple's personal involvement is central to quality
next_steps: Conduct a break-even analysis for a new store in another major city (requires rent, labor, and revenue assumptions)
Pilot a delivery service from the existing Chicago store and measure incremental revenue
Evaluate franchise or licensing structures to scale with lower capital commitment
Survey existing customers to quantify willingness to pay and frequency of repeat visits
